recipes.name: Fried rabbit with garlic
recipes.summary: Rabbit joints marinated in white wine and garlic, fried in olive oil and finished with plenty of garlic: the main course of a fenkata.
method: Joint the rabbit into small pieces and put them in a bowl with the white wine, half the garlic (crushed), the bay leaves, salt and pepper; leave to marinate for at least 2 hours, or overnight in the fridge.
Lift the rabbit out, keeping the marinade, and pat it dry. Heat the olive oil in a wide pan and fry the pieces over a medium heat, turning, for about 20 minutes until golden all over.
Add the rest of the garlic, sliced or as whole peeled cloves, and fry for a couple of minutes until pale gold, taking care it does not burn.
Pour in the strained marinade, cover and cook gently for 20 to 25 minutes until the rabbit is tender, then uncover and let the juices cook down to a garlicky glaze.
Serve hot with patata l-forn or chips.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta on the fenkata (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/a-local-treat-all-you-need-to-know-about-the-traditional-maltese-fenkata), where the rabbit is fried with plenty of garlic and served with chips or roast potatoes. The rabbit line is edible meat without bone, roughly what one rabbit gives; weigh what you can. The wine line counts the wine as poured. Some of the frying oil stays in the pan; all of it is counted. Patata l-forn (Oath's recipe, the whole batch) and chips are optional sides: choose one.

recipes.name: Spaghetti with rabbit sauce
recipes.summary: Spaghetti in a red wine and tomato sauce slow-cooked with rabbit, garlic, bay and peas: the usual first course of a fenkata.
method: Brown the rabbit pieces in the olive oil in a heavy pan, then lift them out.
Soften the chopped onion and garlic in the same pan, stir in the tomato paste for a minute, then pour in the red wine and let it bubble.
Add the chopped tomatoes, bay leaves, salt and pepper, return the rabbit, cover and simmer gently for about 1 hour until the meat comes away from the bones.
Lift out the rabbit, strip the meat from the bones, shred it and stir it back into the sauce with the peas; simmer for 10 minutes more.
Boil the spaghetti until al dente, drain and toss with the sauce; serve with grated parmesan if you like.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta on the fenkata (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/a-local-treat-all-you-need-to-know-about-the-traditional-maltese-fenkata), which describes the sauce as rich tomato with garlic, peas and herbs. In a fenkata the sauce usually comes from the rabbit stew and the meat is served as the main course; this version shreds some rabbit into the sauce so the plate stands alone. The rabbit line is edible meat only, picked from bony pieces such as the forequarters and ribs; weigh what you get. Kunserva is a branded Maltese tomato paste; generic tomato paste is used here.

recipes.name: Gozitan cheeselet ravioli
recipes.summary: Gozitan-style ravioli filled with fresh sheep's milk ġbejniet, egg and parsley instead of ricotta, served in tomato sauce.
method: Mix the flour, semolina, eggs and water into a firm dough, knead for 8 minutes, then cover and rest it for 30 minutes.
Drain the fresh ġbejniet well and mash them with the egg for the filling, the chopped parsley, the pepper and half the dried ġbejna, finely grated.
Roll the dough thinly, dot it with spoonfuls of filling, cover with a second sheet, press out the air around each mound and cut into squares, sealing the edges well.
Warm the tomato sauce. Boil the ravjul in plenty of water for 4 to 5 minutes, lift them out and serve with the sauce and the rest of the dried ġbejna grated over.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/08/07/savouring-gozo-a-culinary-journey-through-mediterranean-flavours-and-traditional-dishes/), which describes Gozitan ravioli filled with sheep's cheese instead of ricotta and served with tomato sauce. The cheeselets are Hanini records: fresh sheep's milk ġbejniet for the filling (drained weight) and dried ġbejniet for grating; swap in your own maker's label if it differs. Fresh ġbejniet are salty, so no salt goes in the filling. The sauce is Oath's tomato pasta sauce component, four of its five portions.

recipes.name: Ricotta pie with peas and broad beans
recipes.summary: Puff pastry pie filled with ricotta, eggs, peas, broad beans, parsley and grated cheese, with optional ham.
method: Heat the oven to 180 °C. Boil the peas and broad beans for 3 minutes, drain, cool and slip the larger broad beans out of their skins.
Press the ricotta through a sieve into a bowl. Beat the eggs with the salt, pepper, chopped parsley and grated parmesan and mix them into the ricotta.
Fold in the peas, the broad beans and the diced ham if using.
Line the pie dish with half the puff pastry, prick the base, add the filling and cover with the rest, sealing the edges; brush the top with the beaten egg to glaze.
Bake for 45 to 50 minutes until deep golden, covering loosely with foil if it browns too fast, and leave to settle for 10 minutes before cutting.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Bald Hiker's Maltese ricotta pie (https://www.baldhiker.com/?p=16654): puff pastry, ricotta, eggs, peas, broad beans, parsley and grated cheese, with optional ham. The pastry line is about two ready-rolled sheets less the trimmings. The cheese can be parmesan, pecorino or grated dried ġbejna. Broad beans are weighed out of the pod; frozen work too.

recipes.name: Maltese meat cakes
recipes.summary: Flat fried patties of beef and pork mince bound with soaked Maltese bread, egg, parsley and grated cheese.
method: Soak the Maltese bread in water for a few minutes, then squeeze it as dry as you can and crumble it into a bowl.
Add the beef mince, pork mince, grated onion, crushed garlic, chopped parsley, eggs, parmesan, salt and pepper and mix well with your hands.
Shape into about 16 flat cakes and coat them in the breadcrumbs.
Shallow-fry in the sunflower oil over a medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes a side until well browned and cooked through, then drain on kitchen paper.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/08/07/savouring-gozo-a-culinary-journey-through-mediterranean-flavours-and-traditional-dishes/), which lists pulpetti as fried savoury patties of meat or fish. The oil line is an estimate of what the cakes take up in a shallow fry, not the whole panful. Some cooks add a little mint or use only beef.

recipes.name: Maltese fish cakes
recipes.summary: Fried cakes of tuna and mashed potato with egg, parsley, mint, capers and lemon zest.
method: Peel the potatoes, boil them until tender, drain well and mash; leave to cool.
Add the drained tuna, the egg, grated onion, crushed garlic, chopped parsley, mint and capers, the lemon zest, flour, salt and pepper and mix well.
Shape into about 16 flat cakes and coat them in the breadcrumbs.
Shallow-fry in the sunflower oil for about 3 minutes a side until golden, then drain on kitchen paper.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/08/07/savouring-gozo-a-culinary-journey-through-mediterranean-flavours-and-traditional-dishes/) for pulpetti of fish or meat, and Apron and Whisk's tuna pulpetti (https://apronandwhisk.com/wprm_print/pulpetti-tat-tonn-taz-zejt-maltese-tuna-fritters) for the tuna and potato base. Tinned tuna in oil is the usual home choice; flaked cooked white fish works too, so swap the line if you use it. The oil line is an estimate of what the cakes take up, not the whole panful.

recipes.name: Oven-baked pork chops with potatoes
recipes.summary: Pork chops rubbed with garlic and fennel seeds and roasted on a tray of Maltese baked potatoes and onions.

lines.unit: p:1 chop without refuse (Yield from 1 raw chop, with refuse, weighing 259g)
lines.label: pork chops

method: Make the patata l-forn in a large roasting dish and bake it covered for the first 40 minutes, as its recipe says.
Meanwhile rub the pork chops with the crushed garlic, fennel seeds, olive oil, salt and pepper.
Uncover the potatoes, lay the chops on top and pour the white wine around them.
Bake at 190 °C for 35 to 40 minutes, turning the chops once, until they are cooked through and the potatoes are golden and have soaked up the juices.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/08/07/savouring-gozo-a-culinary-journey-through-mediterranean-flavours-and-traditional-dishes/), which describes pork chops roasted with potatoes and onions. The potatoes are Oath's patata l-forn, the whole batch of four portions. The chop line is the meat without bone: four loin chops of about 260 g each as bought. The pork juices drip into the potatoes; that fat is already in the chop line.

recipes.name: Steamed beef slices with garlic and parsley
recipes.summary: Thin slices of lean beef layered with garlic, parsley and olive oil on a plate and steamed over a pan of simmering water.
equipment: saucepan for it to sit on
method: Choose a heatproof plate or shallow dish that sits snugly on top of a saucepan, and brush it with a little of the olive oil.

Lay in a layer of the thinly sliced beef, season with salt and pepper and scatter over some of the finely chopped garlic and parsley; repeat the layers, then drizzle with the rest of the oil and the water.
Cover tightly with foil or a second plate, set it over the saucepan of simmering water (or a pot of soup) and steam for 45 minutes to 1 hour until the beef is tender.
Serve with its juices and a squeeze of lemon juice if you like.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes), steamed slices of beef, and Diari l-Bniet (https://diarilbniet.com/2016/10/20/laham-imtektek-fuq-il-fwar-bit-tewn-u-t-tursin/), which layers minute steak with green garlic, parsley, olive oil and a little water; it was the dish made for someone who was ill. The beef is CoFID lean raw topside, the usual cut for minute steak. Green garlic is used in season; ordinary garlic is used here. It can also be baked, covered, in a low oven.

recipes.name: Stuffed aubergines
recipes.summary: Aubergine halves filled with beef mince, their own flesh, egg, parmesan, breadcrumbs and herbs, baked in tomato.
method: Halve the aubergines lengthways, scoop out the flesh leaving a shell about 1 cm thick, and chop the flesh.
Soften the onion and garlic in the olive oil, add the beef mince and brown it, then add the chopped aubergine flesh and the tomato paste and cook for 10 minutes; leave to cool a little.
Mix in the eggs, parmesan, breadcrumbs, chopped parsley and mint, salt and pepper, and pack the filling into the aubergine shells.
Set them in a roasting dish, spoon the chopped tomatoes around and over, cover with foil and bake at 180 °C for 30 minutes, then uncover and bake for 20 to 30 minutes more until tender and browned.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/get-your-bellies-rumbling-here-are-malta-s-favourite-dishes-in-20-pictures), which describes aubergines stuffed with mince and herbs and held together with egg. The aubergine line is the trimmed weight with skin, about four medium aubergines. Kunserva is a branded Maltese tomato paste; generic tomato paste is used here.

recipes.name: Stuffed peppers with olives, capers and anchovies
recipes.summary: Green peppers filled with soaked Maltese bread, tomato, onion, olives, capers, anchovies and herbs, baked in olive oil.
method: Cut the tops off the green peppers, keep them as lids, and pull out the seeds and pith.
Soak the Maltese bread in cold water for a few minutes, squeeze it dry and crumble it into a bowl.
Soften the chopped onion and garlic in half the olive oil, add the chopped tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes.
Mix this into the bread with the chopped anchovies, olives and capers, the parsley, mint and black pepper, and the flaked tuna if using.
Fill the peppers, put the lids back on and stand them in a baking dish with the water and the rest of the oil; bake at 180 °C for 45 to 50 minutes until soft and lightly charred.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes) names bżar mimli as stuffed peppers; the meat-free filling of olives, anchovies, capers, tomatoes, onions and garlic follows TasteAtlas (https://www.tasteatlas.com/malta/appetizers). Many families stuff peppers with mince instead, as for brunġiel mimli. The pepper line is the trimmed weight of four large green peppers. No salt is added: the anchovies, olives and capers bring plenty.

recipes.name: Stuffed squid in tomato sauce
recipes.summary: Whole squid filled with their chopped tentacles, breadcrumbs, anchovies, olives, capers, parsley and egg, then braised in tomato and white wine.
method: Clean the squid, keeping the bodies whole, and finely chop the tentacles and fins.
Mix the chopped tentacles with the breadcrumbs, chopped anchovies, olives and capers, half the garlic, the chopped parsley, the egg, parmesan and pepper.
Spoon the filling loosely into the squid bodies, as it swells while cooking, and close each one with a cocktail stick.
Soften the onion and the rest of the garlic in the olive oil in a wide pan, add the squid and turn them until they firm up, then stir in the tomato paste, pour in the white wine and let it bubble.
Add the chopped tomatoes and salt, cover and simmer gently for 40 to 45 minutes until the squid are tender; slice and serve with the sauce.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes), stuffed calamari, and Rove.me on klamari mimlija (https://rove.me/to/malta/klamari-mimlija-or-stuffed-squid); Maltese fillings vary, usually breadcrumbs and the chopped tentacles with anchovies or tuna, olives and capers, and some use rice. The squid line is the cleaned weight, bodies and tentacles together. Local squid is in season from about November to March.

recipes.name: Octopus with garlic
recipes.summary: Octopus simmered until tender, then tossed in olive oil with plenty of garlic, parsley and a splash of vinegar.
method: Put the cleaned octopus in a large pan with the bay leaf, cover with cold water, bring to the boil and simmer gently for 45 minutes to 1 hour until a knife slides easily into the thickest part; leave it to cool in the liquid.
Drain the octopus and cut it into bite-sized pieces.
Warm the olive oil in a frying pan, add the sliced garlic and the chilli if using, and cook gently until the garlic is pale gold.
Add the octopus and toss over a medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, then add the vinegar, chopped parsley, salt and pepper and serve warm or at room temperature with bread.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes), qarnit bit-tewm, octopus with garlic. Octopus shrinks a great deal as it cooks; the line is the cleaned raw weight. Some cooks finish it with a splash of white wine instead of vinegar. Bread is not included.

recipes.name: Stuffed artichokes
recipes.summary: Globe artichokes with breadcrumbs, anchovies, olives, capers, garlic and parsley pushed between the leaves, simmered upright and finished with olive oil.
equipment: deep saucepan with lid that holds the artichokes upright
method: Cut the stalks off the artichokes so they stand flat, snip off the spiky tips and tap them upside down on the board to open up the leaves; rinse well.
Mix the breadcrumbs with the chopped anchovies, olives, capers, garlic and parsley, the pepper and half the olive oil.
Push the filling down between the leaves and into the centre of each artichoke.
Stand them upright in a deep pan, pour in water to come a third of the way up, drizzle the rest of the olive oil over the tops, cover and simmer for 45 to 50 minutes until a leaf pulls away easily.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's page on Maltese cuisine (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maltese_cuisine), where qaqoċċ mimli is a Lenten dish, and Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/here-s-how-qaqo-mimli-became-malta-s-lenten-classic): breadcrumbs, parsley, olives, capers, garlic and olive oil, often with anchovies or tuna. The artichoke line counts the edible part of four large artichokes (leaf bases and heart), not the tough leaves left on the plate. Leave out the anchovies for a vegetarian version. No salt is added: the anchovies, olives and capers bring plenty.

recipes.name: Maltese arjoli dip
recipes.summary: A rough, egg-free dip of tuna, anchovies, tomato, onion, garlic, herbs, olives, capers and crushed galletti, loosened with olive oil.
method: Crush the galletti to fine crumbs in a bag with a rolling pin.
Mash the drained tuna and the anchovies with the tomato paste, then add the finely chopped fresh tomato, onion, garlic, olives, capers, parsley and mint.
Stir in the crushed galletti, the chilli if using and the pepper, then beat in the olive oil a little at a time until you have a rough, spreadable paste.
Leave for 30 minutes for the flavours to come together and serve with more galletti or bread for dipping.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/bigilla-arjoli-gbejna-9-perfectly-maltese-galletti-toppings-for-the-ultimate-snack-time): tuna, anchovies, tomatoes, garlic, onion and herbs; olives, capers and crushed galletti or breadcrumbs appear in many versions. The catalogue has no galletti record, so plain water biscuits stand in for them. Galletti or bread for dipping are not included; log them separately. Kunserva is a branded Maltese tomato paste; generic tomato paste is used here.

recipes.name: Stuffed olives
recipes.summary: Pitted green olives filled with a paste of tuna, anchovy, capers, bread, garlic and herbs, then marinated in olive oil.
method: Cut the crusts off the bread and blitz it to crumbs in a food processor.
Add the drained tuna, anchovies, capers, garlic, half the parsley, the mint, chilli and black pepper and blend to a smooth paste, adding a spoonful of the olive oil if it is stiff.
Pipe or press a little paste into each of the pitted green olives.
Toss the olives with the rest of the olive oil and parsley, cover and chill overnight; serve at room temperature.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes), pitted green olives stuffed with a tuna mixture, and Apron and Whisk's żebbuġ mimli (https://apronandwhisk.com/wprm_print/zebbug-mimli-stuffed-maltese-olives), which marinates rather than fries them. The olive line is the weight of the pitted olives. Some cooks breadcrumb and fry them; this version is not fried.

recipes.name: Hot chestnut and cocoa drink
recipes.summary: Dried chestnuts simmered with cocoa, sugar, citrus peel, cloves and cinnamon into a thick spiced hot drink, served after Christmas Midnight Mass and on New Year's Eve.
method: Soak the dried chestnuts overnight in plenty of cold water, then drain and pick out any bits of skin left in the folds.
Put them in a large saucepan with the water, bring to the boil and simmer for 30 minutes.
Whisk the cocoa and sugar with a ladle of the hot liquid until smooth, then stir it into the pan with the citrus peel, cloves and cinnamon.

Simmer gently for 30 minutes more, stirring now and then, until the chestnuts are very soft and the liquid has thickened, adding a little hot water if it gets too thick; melt in the dark chocolate at the end if using.
Serve hot in cups or small bowls, with a spoon for the chestnuts.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Guide Me Malta on Malta's Christmas treats (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/yummy-these-are-malta-s-5-favourite-christmas-treats) and Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/04/24/l-imbuljuta-tal-qastan-gozos-favourite-chestnut-christmas-drink/): dried chestnuts, cocoa or chocolate, sugar, tangerine and orange peel, cloves and cinnamon. The chestnut line is CoFID dried chestnuts, weighed before soaking. Tangerine peel is the traditional choice; the catalogue has orange peel, which is close. Whole cloves and a cinnamon stick can replace the ground spices and be lifted out.

recipes.name: Maltese spiced coffee
recipes.summary: Coffee boiled with aniseed, cinnamon and cloves in the old Maltese way, then left to settle and poured off the grounds.
method: Bring 550 ml of water to the boil in a small pan with the aniseed, cinnamon and cloves and let it bubble for 2 minutes.
Stir in 4 heaped tablespoons of ground coffee, bring back just to the boil, then take it off the heat.
Leave to stand for 3 to 4 minutes so the grounds settle, then pour the coffee through a fine strainer into small cups, sweetening with sugar if you like.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): coffee boiled with aniseed, cinnamon sticks and/or rosewater; some use cloves. The coffee line is the brewed drink (filter coffee record), not the grounds, which stay behind. The spice lines are counted although most of them is strained off; they add almost nothing. A piece of cinnamon stick and whole cloves can replace the ground spices; a few drops of rosewater are another old flavouring, not in the catalogue.

recipes.name: Tea in a glass with condensed milk
recipes.summary: Strong black tea poured into a glass over sweetened condensed milk.
method: Brew the strong black tea with one or two tea bags for 4 to 5 minutes.
Spoon the condensed milk into a heatproof glass, pour the tea over and stir until it turns a pale caramel colour; add sugar if you like it sweeter still.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): a local builder's tea, served with condensed milk and sweetened, in a glass. The condensed milk line is about a tablespoon and a half; weigh your usual spoonful once if you drink it often.

recipes.name: Almond drink
recipes.summary: A cold drink of ground almonds simmered with sugar, cinnamon and lemon peel, flavoured with vanilla, sieved and mixed with milk.
method: Put the ground almonds, water, sugar, cinnamon and lemon peel in a saucepan, bring to the boil and simmer for 5 minutes, stirring.
Take off the heat, stir in the vanilla and leave to cool completely.
Blend until smooth, then push it through a fine sieve, pressing well so most of the almond goes through.
Mix the almond syrup with the cold milk and serve over ice.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): cinnamon, vanilla, bitter almonds, sugar, water and milk. The bitter almond note traditionally comes from a few bitter almonds or a drop of bitter almond essence; the catalogue has neither, so it is left out, and it adds almost nothing if you use it. If you strain through muslin and throw away the almond pulp, the drink has less energy than counted here. Many families keep the syrup in the fridge and dilute it with water instead of milk.

recipes.name: Coffee with anisette
recipes.summary: Short black coffee with a measure of anisette stirred in.
method: Make a short, strong coffee and pour it into a small glass or cup.
Stir in the anisette, and the sugar if you take it, and drink while hot.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): coffee with anisette liqueur. The catalogue has no anisette record (usda-all.json has only an anisette biscuit), so the anisette line uses CoFID's average low-to-medium strength liqueur (20 to 28% alcohol), the class sweet anisette belongs to. A stronger anise spirit such as sambuca or pastis has more alcohol and less sugar; swap the line if you use one. The coffee line is a double espresso.

recipes.name: Snails in tomato, garlic and mint sauce
recipes.summary: Small snails boiled, then simmered in a garlicky tomato and red wine sauce with mint and marjoram, and eaten from the shell as a starter or snack.
method: Rinse the snails in several changes of cold water until it runs clear, throwing away any that are empty or smell bad.
Put them in a large pan of cold water, bring slowly to the boil so they come out of their shells, and simmer for 15 minutes, skimming off the froth; drain.
In a wide pan soften the chopped onion and garlic in the olive oil, stir in the tomato paste, then pour in the red wine and let it bubble.
Add the chopped tomatoes, chopped mint, marjoram, chilli, salt and pepper and the snails, cover and simmer for 20 to 30 minutes, adding a splash of water if it gets dry.
Serve hot with cocktail sticks to pick the snails out of their shells, and bread for the sauce.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's page on Maltese cuisine (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maltese_cuisine) and LoveMalta (https://lovemalta.com/its-raining-in-malta-lets-cook-some-snails/), which describes boiling the snails and finishing them in a sauce of tomato, garlic, olive oil and fresh herbs. Snails are usually bought purged and ready to cook. The snail line is the meat out of the shell (Ciqual raw snail); the shells are much of the weight you buy, so this can only be an estimate. Bread is not included.

recipes.name: Stuffed pork flank
recipes.summary: A pocket of pork flank filled with pork mince, breadcrumbs, cheese, parsley and hard-boiled eggs, tied and braised in white wine and tomato with vegetables.
method: Cut a deep pocket along the length of the pork flank with a sharp knife, without cutting through the sides.
Mix the pork mince with the breadcrumbs, parmesan, chopped parsley, raw egg, a third of the finely chopped onion, half the garlic and a little of the salt and pepper.

Spoon half the stuffing into the pocket, lay the hard-boiled eggs along the middle, cover with the rest of the stuffing, then sew or tie the opening closed with butcher's string and season the outside with the remaining salt and pepper.
Brown the meat all over in the olive oil in a large casserole, lift it out and soften the rest of the onion and garlic with the chopped carrots and celery.
Pour in the white wine and let it bubble, add the chopped tomatoes and water, put the meat back, cover and cook at 160 °C for 2 to 2.5 hours, turning once, until very tender.
Rest for 10 minutes, then remove the string, slice and serve with the vegetables and sauce.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes), stuffed flank of pork, and Simon Majumdar's falda (https://www.simonmajumdar.com/falda), which stuffs the flank with pork sausage meat, breadcrumbs, parsley, grated cheese, hard-boiled eggs, onion and garlic and braises it in tomato, stock and wine with carrots and celery. The catalogue has no pork flank record, so this uses CoFID raw pork belly, lean and fat, the part of the pig the flank comes from; ask the butcher to cut the pocket. Skimming fat off the sauce removes some energy that is still counted here. Maltese sausage meat can replace the mince.

recipes.name: Maltese beef broth
recipes.summary: Beef simmered slowly with onion, carrot, celery, tomato, potato, courgette and pumpkin; the broth is served with small pasta and grated cheese, and the meat and vegetables follow.
method: Put the beef in a large pot with the water, bring slowly to the boil and skim off the froth.
Add the onion, carrots, celery, tomato, parsley, salt and pepper and simmer gently, half covered, for 2 hours.
Add the potatoes, courgettes and pumpkin in large chunks and simmer for 40 minutes more until the meat and vegetables are tender.
Lift out the meat and vegetables and keep them warm. Bring the broth back to the boil, add the soup pasta and cook until tender.
Serve the broth and pasta first, with grated parmesan if you like, then the sliced beef and vegetables as a second course.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): beef or chicken broth. The lines count the whole meal, broth, pasta, meat and vegetables; if you have only the broth and pasta, log less. Beef on the bone, such as shin or brisket, is traditional; the line is the meat without bone. Any small soup pasta counts the same as the orzo line.

recipes.name: Maltese chicken broth
recipes.summary: A whole chicken simmered with onion, carrot, celery, tomato, potato, courgette and pumpkin; the broth goes with small pasta and the chicken and vegetables follow.
method: Put the chicken in a large pot with the water, bring slowly to the boil and skim off the froth.
Add the onion, carrots, celery, tomato, parsley, salt and pepper and simmer gently, half covered, for 1 hour.
Add the potatoes, courgettes and pumpkin in large chunks and simmer for 40 minutes more until the chicken and vegetables are tender.
Lift out the chicken and vegetables and keep them warm. Bring the broth back to the boil, add the soup pasta and cook until tender.
Serve the broth and pasta first, with grated parmesan if you like, then the chicken, off the bone, with the vegetables.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): beef or chicken broth. The chicken line is the whole bird weighed with its bones; the app takes the bones off. The lines count the whole meal; if you have only the broth and pasta, log less. Skimming fat off the broth removes some energy that is still counted.

recipes.name: Tomatoes stuffed with rice salad
recipes.summary: Large tomatoes hollowed out and filled with a cold salad of rice, tuna, mayonnaise, olives, capers and parsley: a summer dish.
method: Boil the rice until just tender, adding the peas for the last 3 minutes if using; drain, rinse under cold water and drain well.
Cut a lid off each of the tomatoes, scoop out the seeds and pulp, sprinkle the insides with a little of the salt and turn them upside down to drain.
Mix the cold rice with the flaked tuna, mayonnaise, chopped olives, capers and parsley, the rest of the salt and the pepper.
Fill the tomatoes generously, put the lids back on and chill for 30 minutes before serving.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): a cold summer dish of tomatoes stuffed with cold rice salad, mayonnaise, olives and capers. The tomato line is the shells you eat: eight large tomatoes, about 1.4 kg whole, less the seeds and pulp scooped out. Tuna is a common addition rather than a fixed one.

recipes.name: Broad beans with garlic
recipes.summary: Fresh broad beans boiled and dressed while warm with garlic, olive oil, vinegar, parsley and mint.
method: Boil the shelled broad beans for 5 to 8 minutes until tender, then drain.
Slip the larger beans out of their skins if the skins are tough.
While they are still warm, toss them with the crushed garlic, olive oil, vinegar, chopped parsley and mint, salt and pepper, and leave for 15 minutes before serving.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes), ful bit-tewm. The bean line is weighed out of the pod. In spring the beans are fresh; frozen broad beans work, and out of season dried broad beans, soaked and boiled, are also used (swap the line if you do).

recipes.name: Rice and pumpkin pie
recipes.summary: Shortcrust pie of pumpkin, rice and onion bound with egg and cheese, with tuna, anchovies, olives and marjoram.
method: Make the shortcrust pastry and chill it. Boil the rice for 8 minutes so it is still firm, drain and leave to cool.
Soften the onion in the olive oil, add the pumpkin in small cubes with the marjoram and cook, stirring, for 15 to 20 minutes until soft and starting to break down; leave to cool.
Mix the pumpkin with the rice, flaked tuna, chopped anchovies and olives, two of the eggs, beaten, the parmesan, salt and pepper, and the sultanas if using.
Roll out two thirds of the pastry to line the pie dish, add the filling, cover with the rest and seal; brush with the last of the eggs, beaten.
Bake at 190 °C for 45 to 50 minutes until golden; serve warm or at room temperature.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes), rice and pumpkin pie, and Karmen Tedesco's pumpkin and rice pie on SBS Food (https://www.sbs.com.au/food/recipe/pumpkin-and-rice-pie/7qya7ypji): pumpkin, rice, onion, olives, anchovies and tuna in shortcrust, with sultanas in some families. The pastry is Oath's shortcrust pastry component, one and a half batches; ready-made shortcrust works too. The pumpkin line is peeled, seeded flesh. Leave out the tuna and anchovies for a meat-free pie.

recipes.name: Fried rabbit livers with garlic
recipes.summary: Rabbit livers fried quickly in olive oil with garlic, splashed with white wine and finished with parsley: a fenkata starter.
method: Trim any sinew or green patches from the rabbit livers and pat them dry.
Heat the olive oil in a frying pan, add the sliced garlic and the chilli if using, and cook for a minute without browning.
Add the livers and fry over a high heat for 2 to 3 minutes, turning, until browned outside but still slightly pink inside.
Pour in the white wine and let it bubble for a minute, then season with salt and pepper, scatter over the chopped parsley and serve at once, with Maltese bread for the juices if you like.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Visit Gozo (https://visitgozo.com/2024/08/07/savouring-gozo-a-culinary-journey-through-mediterranean-flavours-and-traditional-dishes/), which lists fried rabbit liver with garlic as a fenkata starter. The liver line is Ciqual's raw rabbit liver. Kidneys and hearts are often cooked the same way alongside; add them as lines if you use them.

recipes.name: Omelette with cheeselets
recipes.summary: A thick Maltese omelette of beaten eggs with crumbled fresh ġbejniet, parsley and black pepper.
method: Beat the eggs with the chopped parsley, black pepper and the salt.
Drain the fresh ġbejniet, crumble them into the eggs and stir gently.
Heat the olive oil in a frying pan, pour in the mixture and cook gently for 6 to 8 minutes until almost set.
Turn it over using a plate and cook for 2 to 3 minutes more, then cut into wedges.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): froġa, an omelette with ġbejna, broad beans or meat. The cheeselets are the Hanini fresh sheep's milk record, two fresh ġbejniet, drained; they are salty, so only a pinch of salt is added. Grated peppered or dried ġbejniet are also used.

recipes.name: Omelette with broad beans
recipes.summary: A thick Maltese omelette of eggs with tender broad beans, onion, parsley, mint and grated cheese.
method: Boil the shelled broad beans for 5 minutes, drain and slip the larger ones out of their skins.
Soften the chopped onion in the olive oil in a frying pan, then add the broad beans and warm through.
Beat the eggs with the parmesan, chopped parsley and mint, salt and black pepper, pour over the beans and cook gently for 6 to 8 minutes until almost set.
Turn it over using a plate and cook for 2 to 3 minutes more, then cut into wedges.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Wikipedia's list of Maltese dishes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Maltese_dishes): froġa, an omelette with ġbejna, broad beans or meat. The broad bean line is weighed out of the pod; frozen beans work too. Grated dried ġbejna can replace the parmesan.

recipes.name: Savoury anchovy fritters
recipes.summary: Puffy yeast-batter fritters with a piece of anchovy hidden inside, deep-fried and served with lemon: a meat-free Lenten treat.
method: Mix the flour, yeast, salt and pepper in a large bowl and beat in the lukewarm water to a thick, sticky batter; cover and leave in a warm place for about 2 hours until doubled and bubbly.
Cut each of the anchovies in half. If using spinach, wilt it, squeeze it dry and chop it; chop the olives if using.
Heat the sunflower oil for deep frying to about 180 °C.
Scoop up a tablespoon of batter, press in a piece of anchovy (with a little spinach and olive if using), cover with a little more batter and slide it into the hot oil with a second spoon.
Fry a few at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until puffed and deep golden; drain on kitchen paper and serve hot, with lemon juice squeezed over if you like.
recipes.notes: AI-written from traditional Maltese practice; not kitchen-tested. Traditional make-up: Apron and Whisk's sfineġ tal-inċova (https://apronandwhisk.com/sfineg-tal-incova-traditional-maltese-anchovy-fritters/) for the yeast batter and anchovy filling, and Guide Me Malta's spring treats (https://www.guidememalta.com/en/6-local-treats-you-have-to-try-this-spring), where savoury sfineġ are stuffed with spinach, anchovies and olives. Makes about 20; a serving is 4. The oil line is an estimate of what the fritters take up, not the fryer's worth.
